To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of the same frequency band for both uplink and downlink is beneficial in terms of spectral efficiency and the use of a flexible duplexing mode is beneficial for the overall system performance.

(i) the use of a single carrier for both downlink and uplink transmissions is a promising candidate for the next generation system, (ii) a hybrid time- and frequency-based scheduler that combines the flexibility of frequency-based and the efficiency of time-based scheduling is a good compromise, and (iii) the design of a flexible, adaptive and efficient interference management and intercell coordination scheme is a key issue to be addressed in the next generation system.

(i) OFDM is the preferred duplexing scheme for next generation wireless networks; (ii) dynamic and flexible resource allocation is a promising candidate for next generation wireless network design; and (iii) a promising approach for interference coordination is the introduction of a virtual cell concept, where a cell is formed by a number of cooperating base stations, and where the cell boundary is defined by the cooperation range.

the design of the next generation wireless systems should be based on a combination of different duplexing schemes and a number of different resource allocation strategies.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the design of the next generation systems should be based on flexible, adaptive and dynamic resource allocation schemes and efficient interference management mechanisms.

duplexing, resource allocation, and inter-cell coordination are three critical issues for the specification of next generation systems, and that there are promising research directions that address these issues.
the design of next-generation systems requires the specification of flexible air interfaces with a high degree of duplexing and scheduling flexibility.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the future generation wireless systems should be designed with flexibility in mind, i.e. with a view towards the possibility of reconfigurability of the system parameters and the possibility for the system to adapt to the changing environment and user requirements.

the future wireless networks will be more complex and will require a more sophisticated system architecture, with the capability of adapting to different scenarios and requirements, in terms of spectrum efficiency, QoS, mobility support, etc.

a combination of multiple duplex modes, a flexible scheduling policy that exploits the multiuser diversity, and a novel approach for interference and inter-cell interference coordination are required for the efficient utilization of the spectrum in the next generation systems.
